title: The Lost Scroll of Baghdad
summary: A young scribe's apprentice at Baghdad's House of Wisdom must find a misplaced Greek scroll before an urgent translation deadline, using his careful knowledge of the library's organization system.
poll: Keeping careful records and organizing a library well is just as important as the scholars' translation work itself.

versions.title: The Lost Scroll of Baghdad
versions.text:
Yusuf is a young scribe. He works at a library. The library is in old Baghdad. People call it the House of Wisdom.

At the library, men copy old scrolls. They make new copies. This keeps old things safe.

One day, a rare scroll is gone. It came from Greece long ago. It is about shapes and stars. The scroll must be copied soon. It must be done in three days. Then it goes back to its owner.

Nasir looks on the shelf. The scroll is not there! He is sad.

Yusuf wants to help. He searches for it. He thinks hard. He knows how the shelves are sorted. Scrolls about stars go on one shelf. Scrolls about the body go on the next shelf.

Yusuf checks the wrong shelf. There it is! Someone made a mistake. They put the scroll in the wrong spot.

Yusuf brings the scroll to Nasir. Now there is time to copy it.

Nasir smiles. He is glad. He tells Yusuf that scribes like him keep old things safe for many years.

versions.title: The Lost Scroll of Baghdad
versions.text:
Yusuf is a young apprentice at the House of Wisdom, a library in ninth-century Baghdad. Scholars gather there from many lands to study and translate.

Every day, Yusuf watches scholars translate old texts from Greek into Arabic. They carefully copy each idea so it will not be lost. The library sorts its scrolls with a catalog system. Each shelf holds scrolls on one subject, and each scroll has a small tag.

One morning, a crisis begins. A rare Greek scroll about shapes and the stars has gone missing from its shelf. The scroll was lent by a merchant who plans to leave Baghdad in three days. It must be translated and copied before then.

Nasir checks the astronomy shelf, but the scroll is not there. He checks the ledger, the book where every borrowed scroll is noted. It shows the scroll was returned days ago.

Yusuf offers to help search. As an apprentice, he has spent many hours learning the catalog system. He remembers that the astronomy and medicine shelves use tags of a similar color.

Sure enough, Yusuf finds the scroll misplaced on the medicine shelf. Another apprentice must have set it there by mistake.

Nasir is deeply relieved, and the work begins. He praises Yusuf for knowing the system so well, and reminds him how much careful order matters.

versions.title: The Lost Scroll of Baghdad
versions.text:
Yusuf is a young apprentice at the House of Wisdom, a library and center of learning in ninth-century Baghdad, where scholars from Persia, India, and the Byzantine world gathered to study and translate ancient manuscripts.

Every day, Yusuf watched scholars translate manuscripts from Greek into Arabic, meticulously copying each idea onto fresh paper so that invaluable knowledge would be preserved rather than lost. The library's archive sorted its scrolls using a careful catalog system: each shelf held manuscripts on a single subject, and each scroll carried a small colored tag showing where it belonged.

One especially tense morning, a crisis began. A rare Greek manuscript about geometry and the movement of the stars had gone missing from its shelf. The manuscript had been lent by a traveling merchant who intended to leave Baghdad within three days, so it had to be translated and copied before he departed.

Nasir checked the astronomy shelf first, but the manuscript simply was not there. He then consulted the ledger, the record book where every borrowed item was meticulously logged. It clearly showed the manuscript had been returned days earlier, which puzzled him.

Yusuf offered to help search rather than wait anxiously. As an apprentice, he had spent countless hours mastering the archive's catalog system, and he recalled that the astronomy shelf and the medicine shelf used nearly identical colored tags, a detail that could easily confuse anyone in haste.

Sure enough, Yusuf found the manuscript misplaced among the medicine scrolls, where another careless apprentice had evidently set it down while hastily reshelving a stack of texts.

Nasir was deeply relieved, and the translation work began at once. He praised Yusuf for understanding the archive's system so thoroughly, reminding him that this kind of preserving work was exactly how earlier scholars had kept ancient Greek science alive for others.

Yusuf, a young apprentice at the House of Wisdom, worked at one of the most renowned libraries and centers of learning in ninth-century Baghdad, where scholars from Persia, India, and the Byzantine world gathered to study and translate ancient manuscripts into Arabic for generations not yet born.

Every day, Yusuf observed scholars translate manuscripts from Greek into Arabic, meticulously copying each idea onto fresh paper, a craft that had only recently arrived from China, ensuring that invaluable knowledge would be preserved rather than lost to neglect or careless handling. The library's archive organized its scrolls through a careful catalog system: each shelf held manuscripts devoted to a single subject, and each scroll carried a small colored tag indicating precisely where it belonged.

One especially tense morning, a crisis unfolded. A rare Greek manuscript about geometry and the movement of celestial bodies had vanished from its shelf. The manuscript had been lent by a traveling merchant who intended to depart Baghdad within three days, so it absolutely had to be translated and copied in full before his departure, with no room for delay.

Nasir checked the astronomy shelf first, but the manuscript simply was not there. He then consulted the ledger, the record book where every borrowed item was meticulously logged by the librarians, yet it clearly indicated the manuscript had already been returned days earlier.

Yusuf offered to help search rather than wait anxiously alongside the others. As an apprentice, he had devoted countless hours to mastering the archive's catalog system, and he recalled that the astronomy shelf and the medicine shelf happened to employ nearly identical colored tags, a seemingly minor detail that could easily confuse anyone working in haste.

Sure enough, Yusuf located the manuscript misplaced among the medicine scrolls, where another careless apprentice had evidently deposited it while hastily reshelving a stack of texts earlier that same week.

Nasir was profoundly relieved, and the translation work commenced at once. He commended Yusuf for understanding the archive's system so thoroughly, reminding him that this sort of preserving work was precisely how earlier scholars had kept ancient Greek science alive for the wider world to inherit and study.

versions.title: The Lost Scroll of Baghdad
versions.text:
Yusuf, a young apprentice at the House of Wisdom, worked within one of the most renowned libraries and centers of learning in ninth-century Baghdad, where scholars from Persia, India, and the Byzantine world converged to study and translate ancient manuscripts into Arabic for generations not yet born, extending knowledge far beyond the city's own walls and into later centuries.

Every day, Yusuf observed scholars translate manuscripts from Greek into Arabic, meticulously copying each idea onto fresh paper, a craft only recently arrived from China, ensuring that invaluable knowledge would be preserved rather than lost to the ravages of neglect or careless handling. The library's archive organized its collection through a careful catalog system, in which each shelf held manuscripts devoted to a single subject and each scroll carried a small colored tag indicating precisely where it belonged.

The crisis began on an especially tense morning, when a rare Greek manuscript about geometry and the movement of celestial bodies vanished from its customary shelf. The manuscript had been lent by a traveling merchant who intended to depart Baghdad within three days, meaning it absolutely had to be translated and copied in its entirety before his departure, with no possibility of extension of any kind.

Nasir checked the astronomy shelf first, only to discover the manuscript was simply not there, and a subsequent search of the ledger, the record book where every borrowed item was meticulously logged, revealed that the manuscript had already been returned to the library days earlier, deepening the mystery considerably.

Yusuf offered to help search rather than wait anxiously alongside the others, who seemed increasingly resigned to watching the deadline slip away. Having devoted countless hours to mastering the archive's catalog system, he recalled that the astronomy shelf and the medicine shelf employed nearly identical colored tags, a seemingly minor detail capable of confusing anyone working in considerable haste.

Sure enough, Yusuf located the manuscript misplaced among the medicine scrolls, evidently deposited there by another careless apprentice who had been hastily reshelving a stack of texts earlier that week without ever noticing the error.

Nasir, profoundly relieved, set the translation work in motion at once, commending Yusuf for understanding the archive's system so thoroughly and reminding him that this sort of preserving work was precisely how earlier scholars had kept ancient Greek science alive for the wider world to inherit, study, and build upon for many years, and even centuries, to come.

versions.text:
Yusuf, a young apprentice at the House of Wisdom, worked within one of the most renowned libraries and centers of learning in ninth-century Baghdad, where scholars from Persia, India, and the Byzantine world converged to study and translate ancient manuscripts into Arabic for generations not yet born, extending the reach of knowledge far beyond the city's own walls and into centuries to come.

Every day, Yusuf observed scholars translate manuscripts from Greek into Arabic, meticulously copying each idea onto fresh paper, a craft only recently introduced from China, ensuring that invaluable knowledge would be preserved rather than lost to the ravages of neglect or careless handling by less disciplined hands. The library's archive organized its collection through a careful catalog system, in which each shelf held manuscripts devoted to a single subject and each scroll carried a small colored tag indicating precisely where it belonged within the wider collection.

The crisis began on an especially tense morning, when a rare Greek manuscript about geometry and the movement of celestial bodies vanished from its customary shelf. The manuscript had been lent by a traveling merchant who intended to depart Baghdad within three days, meaning it absolutely had to be translated and copied in its entirety before his departure, with no realistic possibility of an extension.

Nasir checked the astronomy shelf first, only to discover the manuscript was simply not there, and a subsequent, increasingly urgent search of the ledger, the record book where every borrowed item was meticulously logged, revealed that the manuscript had already been returned to the library days earlier, which only deepened the mystery surrounding its disappearance.

Yusuf offered to help search rather than wait anxiously alongside the others, who seemed increasingly resigned to watching the deadline slip irretrievably away. Having devoted countless hours to mastering the archive's catalog system, he recalled that the astronomy shelf and the medicine shelf employed nearly identical colored tags, a seemingly minor detail nonetheless capable of confusing anyone working in considerable haste.

Sure enough, Yusuf located the manuscript misplaced among the medicine scrolls, evidently deposited there by another careless apprentice who had been hastily reshelving a stack of texts earlier that week without ever noticing his own error.

Nasir, profoundly relieved, set the translation work in motion immediately, commending Yusuf for understanding the archive's system so thoroughly and reminding him that this sort of preserving work was precisely how earlier scholars had kept ancient Greek science alive for the wider world to inherit, study, and build upon across many centuries to come, long after the scholars who did this careful work were gone from the world.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who learns to copy letters for the first time in a school by the river
A merchant who sells scrolls in the market of a big city
An apprentice who finds a missing scroll before an important deadline
A library that moves to a new building across the river
questions.why: The story follows Yusuf as he searches for a missing scroll and finds it in time to be copied before its deadline.

wrong.A: Yusuf already knows how to copy; the story is about finding the scroll.
wrong.B: The merchant only owns the scroll; he does not sell it in a market in the story.
wrong.D: The library does not move to a new building in the story.

questions.stem: Where does Yusuf work?
options: At a school in Damascus for boys
At a merchant's house in Cairo
At a shop that sells paper in town
At the House of Wisdom in Baghdad
questions.why: In the story, Yusuf works in the library in old Baghdad called the House of Wisdom.

wrong.A: The story does not mention Damascus.
wrong.B: Yusuf works at the library, not at the merchant's house.
wrong.C: Yusuf works at a library, not a paper shop.

questions.stem: What is the missing scroll about?

The life of a traveling merchant

wrong.A: The scroll is not about cooking or food.
wrong.C: The scroll is not about building libraries.
wrong.D: The scroll is about science ideas, not the merchant's life.

questions.stem: In the story, a scribe is someone who —
options: writes or copies things by hand
sells scrolls to merchants
builds shelves for a library
travels from city to city
questions.why: The story shows scribes copying old scrolls into new copies, so a scribe is a person who writes or copies things by hand.

wrong.B: The story does not say scribes sell scrolls.
wrong.C: Scribes copy texts; they do not build shelves.
wrong.D: The merchant travels, not the scribe.

questions.stem: Why did the scroll need to be copied within three days?
options: Because the scroll would fall apart after three days
Because Scholar Nasir was leaving the library forever
Because it had to go back to its owner after that time
Because Yusuf wanted a new scroll for himself
questions.why: In the story, the scroll must be copied within three days because then it goes back to its owner.

wrong.A: The story does not say the scroll would fall apart.
wrong.B: Scholar Nasir was not leaving the library.
wrong.D: Yusuf was not trying to keep a scroll for himself.

questions.stem: What can you tell about why Yusuf could find the scroll quickly?
options: He used a map that Scholar Nasir gave him at the door of the library
He asked the traveling merchant where it was in the hall
He guessed randomly and he got very lucky that day
He already knew exactly how the library's shelves were sorted
questions.why: The story says Yusuf knew how the library sorts its scrolls, which is why he could check the right places and find it.

wrong.B: The merchant is not shown helping search for the scroll.
wrong.C: Yusuf used his knowledge of the shelves, not a random guess.

questions.stem: Why was the scroll on the wrong shelf?
options: Someone put it back in the wrong place by mistake
The scroll walked there on its own
Scholar Nasir hid it there on purpose
The merchant moved it there to keep it safe

wrong.B: Scrolls cannot move by themselves.
wrong.C: Scholar Nasir was worried about the scroll, not hiding it.
wrong.D: The merchant is not shown moving the scroll.

questions.stem: Why does the author show Yusuf thinking calmly instead of panicking?
options: To show that Yusuf does not care about the scroll or the library
To show that staying calm and thinking helps solve problems
To show that Scholar Nasir cannot be trusted by anyone
To show that libraries are not useful places for students
questions.why: Because Yusuf stays calm and thinks through the shelf system, he is able to find the scroll in time, showing the value of careful thinking.

wrong.A: Yusuf clearly cares, since he works hard to help.
wrong.C: Scholar Nasir is shown as a careful, trustworthy scholar.

wrong.B: The article shows apprentices, including Yusuf, doing valuable work.
wrong.D: Scholar Nasir follows the library's system carefully.

questions.stem: Because the ledger showed the scroll had already been returned, what did Scholar Nasir need to do next?
options: Add a new rule banning apprentices from the shelves of the library
Ask the merchant to send a brand-new scroll from his shop in town
Cancel the translation project completely and send all the workers home
Search the library physically instead of assuming it was still out on loan
questions.why: Since the ledger showed the scroll was back, the problem had to be inside the library, which is why Yusuf began searching the shelves.

wrong.A: No such rule is mentioned in the article.
wrong.B: A new scroll was not requested; the original scroll was needed.
wrong.C: The project continued once the scroll was found.

questions.stem: How does the author structure the article?
options: By describing the problem, then the investigation, then the resolution
By comparing two different libraries in two different cities, one old and one new
By listing every subject kept in the House of Wisdom, one after another
By explaining the life story of the traveling merchant, from birth to old age
questions.why: The article first presents the missing-scroll problem, then shows Yusuf's investigation using the catalog system, then ends with the scroll being found.

wrong.B: Only one library, the House of Wisdom, is described.
wrong.C: The article does not list every subject in the library.
wrong.D: The merchant's life story is not described.

MID.prompt: Explain how the library's catalog system helped Yusuf find the missing scroll. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the catalog system helped.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The library's catalog system helped Yusuf find the missing scroll in two important ways. First, because he knew that each shelf held scrolls on one subject, he understood the scroll had to be somewhere nearby, not truly lost. Second, he remembered that the astronomy and medicine shelves used nearly identical colored tags, which told him exactly where to check. Using this knowledge, he found the scroll misplaced among the medicine scrolls and brought it back in time.

keyWords.definition: a document written by hand, especially an old or valuable one
keyWords.example: The historian carefully photographed every page of the ancient manuscript.

keyWords.definition: to protect something so it stays safe and does not get damaged or lost
keyWords.example: Cold temperatures help preserve food for a longer time.

keyWords.definition: extremely careful and paying close attention to small details
keyWords.example: The jeweler was meticulous when fixing the tiny watch parts.

keyWords.definition: so useful or important that its value cannot really be measured
keyWords.example: Her advice before the exam turned out to be invaluable.

keyWords.definition: a collection of historical documents or records kept in an organized way
keyWords.example: Researchers found old letters in the city's archive.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The House of Wisdom was only a storage room with no real organization at all.
Scholar Nasir translated the whole manuscript by himself before Yusuf ever arrived.
Dedicated apprentices and careful archives let Baghdad's scholars preserve ancient science.
The traveling merchant personally organized every shelf inside the library himself.
questions.why: The article shows how the archive's catalog system, the ledger, and Yusuf's careful knowledge all combined to preserve and translate an important manuscript.

wrong.A: The article describes a careful catalog system, not a disorganized storage room.
wrong.B: The translation work could only begin once Yusuf found the manuscript.
wrong.D: The merchant only lent the manuscript; the library's own staff organized the shelves.

questions.stem: What material had only recently reached Baghdad and was used for copying manuscripts?
options: Clay tablets from ancient Greece
Thin sheets of metal from Persia
Cloth imported from the Byzantine world
Paper, a craft newly arrived from China
questions.why: Scholars copied books onto fresh sheets of paper, which had only recently arrived.

wrong.A: Clay tablets are not mentioned; paper is the material described.
wrong.B: Metal sheets are not mentioned as a copying material.
wrong.C: Cloth is not described as a writing material in the article.

questions.stem: In the article, the word invaluable means —
options: worth nothing at all to anyone in the world, now or in the future
so useful or important that its value cannot really be measured
borrowed for exactly three days from the library
written only in Greek by the old scholars of Athens
questions.why: The article describes the knowledge in the manuscripts as invaluable, meaning extremely important and valuable.

wrong.A: Invaluable means extremely valuable, the opposite of worthless.
wrong.C: The three-day deadline is a separate detail, not the meaning of invaluable.
wrong.D: Invaluable describes importance, not language.

questions.stem: According to the ledger, what should have already happened to the manuscript?
options: It should have already been returned to the library
It should have already been destroyed by accident
It should have already been sold to another merchant
It should have already been translated into Greek
questions.why: The ledger showed the manuscript had already been returned to the library several days earlier, which deepened the mystery of its disappearance.

wrong.B: Nothing in the article suggests the manuscript was destroyed.
wrong.C: No sale to another merchant is mentioned.
wrong.D: The manuscript needed to be translated from Greek, not into it.

questions.stem: Why was the similarity between the astronomy and medicine shelf tags especially risky for the archive?
options: It meant scholars could no longer read Greek at all, and many books were burned
It meant the merchant could easily steal manuscripts, and nobody would notice
It meant rare, hard-to-replace manuscripts could seem lost even while physically present
It meant the library had to close for repairs, and the apprentices lost their jobs
questions.why: Because the manuscript was simply shelved in the wrong place, the similar tags nearly caused a valuable, irreplaceable manuscript to go unfound before its deadline.

wrong.A: The scholars could still read and translate Greek throughout the article.
wrong.B: The mix-up is described as an honest mistake, not theft.
wrong.D: No closing or repairs are mentioned.

questions.stem: Which of these shows the correct order of events?
options: The manuscript is found first, and only then does the merchant lend it out
The ledger is checked, the merchant lends it, and then Yusuf finds the manuscript
Yusuf finds the manuscript, then it goes missing, then the merchant lends it
The merchant lends it, it goes missing, the ledger is checked, Yusuf finds it
questions.why: The manuscript was first lent by the merchant, then discovered missing, then the ledger was checked, and finally Yusuf located it on the wrong shelf.

wrong.A: The manuscript had to go missing before anyone could find it.
wrong.B: The merchant lent the manuscript before the ledger was checked about it.
wrong.C: The manuscript could not go missing before it was ever lent.

questions.stem: What does Scholar Nasir's comment to Yusuf at the end suggest about the broader purpose of the House of Wisdom's work?
options: That meticulous organization, not just translation itself, helped ancient science reach later generations
That translation work is unimportant compared to simply owning old manuscripts in a large library
That only merchants deserve credit for preserving knowledge, since they brought books from far lands
That apprentices should avoid handling valuable manuscripts, because they are too young and careless
questions.why: Scholar Nasir links Yusuf's careful, organized searching directly to how earlier scholars kept ancient science alive, showing organization matters alongside translation.

wrong.B: The article values translation highly, not just ownership.
wrong.C: The merchant only lends the manuscript; scholars and apprentices do the preserving work.
wrong.D: Yusuf's careful handling of the manuscript is praised, not discouraged.

questions.stem: Why does the author emphasize that the manuscript 'had already been returned' according to the ledger?
options: To prove that the ledger was completely useless to the library and its keepers
To show that careful records alone cannot guarantee an item ends up in the right place
To suggest that the merchant lied about returning it, though no one could prove it
To explain why paper is better than clay tablets for keeping a record of loans
questions.why: The ledger correctly recorded the return, yet the manuscript was still misplaced, showing that systems still depend on people being careful with physical items.

wrong.A: The ledger actually gave Scholar Nasir an important clue, so it was useful.
wrong.C: The article does not suggest the merchant lied.
wrong.D: The article is not comparing paper and clay tablets at this point.

HIGH.prompt: The article shows how careful organization and translation work helped preserve ancient science. Do you think this kind of careful, detailed work is as important as the discoveries themselves? Support your argument with evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the question.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe careful, detailed work is just as important as the original discoveries themselves. The article shows that even though the Greek manuscript contained valuable ideas about geometry and the stars, that knowledge nearly stayed lost inside the library simply because of a shelving mistake. Someone might argue that the ideas inside the manuscript matter more than where it sits on a shelf. However, without Yusuf's meticulous knowledge of the archive's catalog system, the manuscript might never have been translated and copied before the merchant's deadline, meaning the ideas themselves could have been lost to later generations entirely.

a plan to build

MID.stem: Why must the scroll be translated within three days?

Nasir plans to travel
The scroll will fall apart

options: He had seen it on the medicine shelf

He asked the merchant for help

HIGH.stem: In the article, the word hastily most nearly means —
options: very slowly
in a rush
with great joy
